great-mother.line: Jung drew a line between the Great Mother, a figure of comparative religion, and the mother archetype behind it. Neumann, his student, gave the archetype its fullest single study. This page holds both, then the images, the instances and the dreams the field has for it.

sections.title: The archetype and the image
sections.line: Jung keeps the Great Mother, the goddess of the religions, apart from the mother archetype it comes from. The archetype itself is never seen; only its images are.

quotes.text: The concept itself is of no immediate concern to psychology, because the image of a Great Mother in this form is rarely encountered in practice, and then only under very special conditions.

sections.line: Every account of her holds both a giving and a devouring side, and refuses to split them into two figures.

sections.title: Her structure
sections.line: Neumann reads two characters in the Feminine: one that holds and keeps, one that changes. Her central symbol is the vessel.

quotes.text: The elementary character of the Feminine becomes evident wherever the ego and consciousness are still small and undeveloped and the unconscious is dominant.

In the transformative character, the accent is on the dynamic element of the psyche, which, in contrast to the conservative tendency of the elementary character, drives toward motion, change, and, in a word, transformation.
we arrive at a universal symbolic formula for the early period of mankind: Woman = body = vessel = world

sections.title: Where she stands in the growth of consciousness
sections.line: In Origins, Neumann puts the Great Mother at the start of a sequence: the ego held in the unconscious, then slowly freed from it, until the hero. Jung wrote the book's foreword.

quotes.text: The mythological stages in the evolution of consciousness begin with the stage when the ego is contained in the unconscious
The positive side of the Great Mother seems to be embodied in this stage of the uroboros.
The Great Mother takes the little child back into herself, and always, over uroboric incest there stand the insignia of death, signifying final dissolution in union with the Mother.
While yet in the fold of the creation myth it enters upon the second cycle, namely, the hero myth
It begins just where I, too, if I were granted a second lease of life, would start to gather up the disjecta membra of my own writings
